dervis-irab:1-15.t:
* Vocabulary:
(وَأَذِنَتْ): it listened to His command. One says "adhintu laka," i.e. I listened to your speech. In the Ḥadīth: "Allah has not listened to anything as He listens to a prophet chanting the Qur'an melodiously." The poet said: "Deaf, when they hear good mentioned of them; but if they are mentioned with evil among them, they listen."
In al-Mukhtār: "adhina lahu: he listened; its pattern is ṭariba, and from it the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿وَأَذِنَتْ لِرَبِّها وَحُقَّتْ﴾." One says adhina yaʾdhanu adhanan ilayhi and lahu: he listened to it admiringly, or generally; and of the smell of food, he desired it. Adhina bi-l-shayʾ (like samiʿa), idhnan (with kasra, or with vowelling) and adhānan and adhānatan: he knew of it; fa-ʾdhanū bi-ḥarb means "be aware of war." Ādhanahu al-amr and bihi: he informed him. Adhdhana tāʾdhīnan: he made much announcement. Of a person: he rubbed his ear and turned him back from drinking, so he did not give him to drink; of a sandal and the like: he made an ear for it. "He did it with my idhn and adhīn," i.e. with my knowledge. Adhina lahu fī al-shayʾ (like samiʿa), idhnan (with kasra) and adhīnan: he permitted it to him. Istaʾdhanahu: he asked his permission... and so on to the end of this wondrous root.
(كادِحٌ): striving in your work. Al-kadḥ is the exertion of the soul in work and toil in it until it leaves a mark on it, from kadaḥa jildahu, when he scratched it. In al-Mukhtār: "al-kadḥ is work, effort, toil and earning, and it is also scratching, the pattern of all of it being qaṭaʿa. And the words of Allah the Exalted ﴿إِنَّكَ كادِحٌ إِلى رَبِّكَ﴾ mean striving; wa-bi-wajhihi kudūḥ means scratches; huwa yakdaḥu li-ʿiyālihi wa-yaktadiḥu: he earns." Among the curiosities of the kāf and dāl is that when they occur as the first and middle letters of a word, they indicate exertion, perseverance and effect. One says "so-and-so is kadūd": he drives himself in work and wearies himself. By figurative usage: kadda lisānahu bi-l-kalām and qalbahu bi-l-fikr; kaddat al-dawābb al-arḍ bi-l-ḥawāfir, and it is al-kadīd; and kardtu raʾsī wa-jildī bi-l-aẓfār when I scratched it with insistent scratching. From this is the saying of Kuthayyir:
غنيت فلم أرددكم عن بغيّة ... وجعت فلم أكددكم بالأصابع
(I was self-sufficient and did not turn you away from any desire, and I was hungry and did not drive you with my fingers.)
that is, I did not press you with requests. A well from which water is not reached except with exertion is called kadūd; likewise a she-camel kadūd and a man kadūd: his milk and his good are not obtained except after hardship. Ibn Hubayra used to say: "Kuddūnī, for I am mukidd," that is, ask me, for I give upon request. Kadira al-māʾ, on the authority of Ibn al-Aʿrābī, has the three forms; māʾ akdar and kadir is plainly turbid. By figurative usage: kadira ʿaynuhu and takaddara; "take what is clear and leave what is turbid"; kadira ʿalayya fulān, and he is kadir al-fuʾād toward me. He said:
وإني لمشتاق إلى ظل صاحب ... يرق ويصفو إن كدرت عليه
(I long for the shade of a companion who softens and grows clear when I am clouded toward him.)
And "he has a kuds of food" and akdās. Al-Mutalammis said:
لم تدر بصرى بما آليت من قسم ... ولا دمشق إذا ديس الكداديس
(Buṣrā did not know of the oath I swore, nor Damascus when the heaps were trodden.)
He meant al-akdās, and it is a collective noun. Kadasa al-ṭaʿām fa-takaddasa: heaping up food, and what is in it of weight and effort is not hidden. Kadamahu: he bit him with the edge of the mouth, and ḥimār mukaddam means bitten. And "he is dhū kudna and ʿabāla," meaning thickness and heaviness, and from this is al-kawdan, the Turkish pack-horse. Akdā al-ḥāfir: the hoof reached al-kudya, the hardness of the ground, which stopped it, like their saying ajbala al-ḥāfir. By figurative usage akdā al-rajul: he failed and did not obtain his need; and "so-and-so is mukidd, his wealth does not grow"... and so on to the end of what came from this root.
(ثُبُوراً): al-thubūr is destruction. In al-Miṣbāḥ: "thabara Allāh al-kāfir thubūran (of the pattern qaʿada): He destroyed him; and thabara huwa thubūran: he perished; it is both transitive and intransitive."
(يَحُورَ): to return. Al-Rāghib said: al-ḥawr is hesitation in a matter, and from it "we seek refuge in Allah from al-ḥawr after al-kawr," that is, from hesitation in a matter after having proceeded in it; muḥāwarat al-kalām is exchanging it back and forth; and al-ḥawr is the wood on which the pulley runs because it goes back and forth upon it. In al-Mukhtār: "ḥāra: he returned, and its pattern is qāla and dakhala"; the maṣdar is on the pattern qawl and dukhūl; one says ḥawran, ḥuʾūran, maḥāran and maḥāratan. Further, ḥāra comes in the sense of ṣāra (became), taking a nominative noun and an accusative predicate.

* I'rab:
(إِذَا السَّماءُ انْشَقَّتْ وَأَذِنَتْ لِرَبِّها وَحُقَّتْ): إذا is an adverbial for future time; السَّماءُ is the agent of an omitted verb that what follows explains, the implied form being "when the sky splits, it splits," because conditional إذا is specifically entered before verbal clauses, and whatever comes in this form and the like is interpreted to preserve the rule of specificity, as was discussed in detail in Sūrat al-Takwīr. The clause انْشَقَّتْ is explicative, with no grammatical position; the omitted clause انْشَقَّتْ is in the position of a genitive by the annexation of the adverbial to it. The apodosis of إذا is omitted; it was omitted to alert that it is something description cannot encompass, or so that the imagination may go every way. It was also said that its apodosis is what is indicated by فَمُلاقِيهِ, i.e. when the sky splits, man meets his toil. It was also said it has no apodosis, being accusative as the object of an omitted "mention" (udhkur), and so it is not conditional. The wāw is a conjunction; أَذِنَتْ is a past verb; لِرَبِّها is attached to أَذِنَتْ, i.e. it listened to Him; وحُقَّتْ is a passive past verb. Know that the agent in this construction is Allah the Exalted, i.e. Allah made that due upon it, that is, its hearing and obedience; one says "he is fit (ḥaqīq) for such" and "he is entitled to it." The meaning is "it was fitting for it to do that." So the agent is omitted, namely Allah the Exalted, and the direct object is its hearing and obedience, which is not mentioned; the attribution in the verse is to the sky itself, so it needs an implied element, the implied form being "and it was made due," i.e. its hearing and obedience was made due, that is, Allah the Exalted made it due upon it, obligated it and bound it to it. This is the apparent sense. Al-Bayḍāwī allowed that the deputy agent be the pronoun of the sky latent in the verb, without implying anything; his words: "wa-ḥuqqat means 'it was made worthy of listening and submission.'" (وَإِذَا الْأَرْضُ مُدَّتْ، وَأَلْقَتْ ما فِيها وَتَخَلَّتْ وَأَذِنَتْ لِرَبِّها وَحُقَّتْ): a conjunction to what precedes, similar to it in its i'rab. (يا أَيُّهَا الْإِنْسانُ إِنَّكَ كادِحٌ إِلى رَبِّكَ كَدْحاً فَمُلاقِيهِ): يا is a vocative particle; أَيُّ is an indefinite particular noun addressed, indeclinable on damma in the position of an accusative; the hāʾ is for alerting; الْإِنْسانُ is a badal; إن and its noun; كادِحٌ is its predicate; إِلى رَبِّكَ is attached to كادِحٌ. "إلى" here has the meaning of limit, i.e. the limit of your toil in good and evil ends in meeting your Lord, which is death. كَدْحاً is an absolute object (mafʿūl muṭlaq); the fāʾ is a conjunction; مُلاقِيهِ is conjoined to كادِحٌ, and it may be the predicate of an omitted mubtadaʾ, i.e. "so you are meeting it"; on the first view it is a conjoining of a single word to a single word, on the second a conjoining of clauses. (فَأَمَّا مَنْ أُوتِيَ كِتابَهُ بِيَمِينِهِ): the fāʾ is resumptive; أما is a particle of condition and detailing; مَنْ is a relative noun, mubtadaʾ; the clause أُوتِيَ is a ṣila with no position, and the deputy agent is a latent pronoun referring to مَنْ; كِتابَهُ is a second direct object; بِيَمِينِهِ is attached to أُوتِيَ. (فَسَوْفَ يُحاسَبُ حِساباً يَسِيراً): the fāʾ links to the apodosis of أما; سَوْفَ is a particle of futurity; يُحاسَبُ is an imperfect passive verb whose deputy agent is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "he"; حِساباً is an absolute object and يَسِيراً is a naʿt of حِساباً. (وَيَنْقَلِبُ إِلى أَهْلِهِ مَسْرُوراً): the wāw is a conjunction; يَنْقَلِبُ is an imperfect verb in the nominative whose agent is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "he"; إِلى أَهْلِهِ is attached to يَنْقَلِبُ; مَسْرُوراً is a ḥāl; and the clause سَوْفَ يُحاسَبُ is the khabar of مَنْ. (وَأَمَّا مَنْ أُوتِيَ كِتابَهُ وَراءَ ظَهْرِهِ فَسَوْفَ يَدْعُوا ثُبُوراً): a conjunction to the preceding clause, similar to it in i'rab. وَراءَ ظَهْرِهِ is accusative by removal of the preposition, i.e. he is given his book in his left hand from behind his back; the fāʾ links; the clause سَوْفَ يَدْعُوا ثُبُوراً is the khabar of مَنْ, and ثُبُوراً is the object of يَدْعُوا, i.e. he calls out for his destruction saying "yā thubūrāh," because calling on what is not rational is meant as a wish; so the "call" (duʿāʾ) here means a request by vocative. (وَيَصْلى سَعِيراً): conjoined to يَدْعُوا, and سَعِيراً is the object of يَصْلى. (إِنَّهُ كانَ فِي أَهْلِهِ مَسْرُوراً): a reason for what he meets; إن and its noun; the clause كان is its predicate; فِي أَهْلِهِ is a ḥāl and مَسْرُوراً is the predicate of كان. (إِنَّهُ ظَنَّ أَنْ لَنْ يَحُورَ): a second reason; إن and its noun; the clause ظَنَّ is its predicate; ظن here means knowledge and certainty; أن is the lightened form of the heavy أن and its noun is the pronoun of the situation (ḍamīr al-shaʾn); لن is a particle of negation, accusative and futurity; يَحُورَ is an imperfect verb put in the accusative by لن; the clause لَنْ يَحُورَ is the predicate of أن, and أن with what is within its scope fills the place of the two objects of ظَنَّ. (بَلى إِنَّ رَبَّهُ كانَ بِهِ بَصِيراً): بَلى is a particle of reply affirming what follows a negation; إن and its noun; the clause كان is its predicate; بِهِ is attached to بَصِيراً and بَصِيراً is the predicate of كان; the clause of إن with what is within its scope is the response to an implied oath, or a reason for the affirmation of what follows لن that بَلى conveys.

* Rhetoric:
1- In «وأذنت لربها وحقّت» there is a metaphor with the likened-to omitted (istiʿāra makniyya): the state of the sky in its submission to the effect of Allah the Exalted's power, when He wished it to split, is likened to the submission of an obedient listener to a command; then the likened-to is omitted and the word for listening and hearing, used for its goal, is borrowed.
2- In «وألقت ما فيها وتخلت» there is a metaphor with the likened-to omitted (istiʿāra makniyya): the state of the earth is likened to that of a pregnant woman who casts out what is in her belly under hardship and terror; then the likened-to is omitted and the word for casting out is borrowed.

dervis-irab:16-25.t:
* Vocabulary:
(الشفق): Al-Zamakhsharī said: "al-shafaq is the redness seen in the west after the sun has set; with its disappearance the time of Maghrib ends and the time of ʿatama (the Ishāʾ prayer) begins, according to the generality of scholars, except what is reported from Abū Ḥanīfa in one of two narrations, that it is the whiteness; Asad ibn ʿAmr reported that he retracted it. It was named shafaq because of its fineness (riqqa); from it comes al-shafaqa for a person, which is tenderness of heart toward him." Al-Rāghib said: "al-shafaq is the mingling of the light of day with the blackness of night at sunset; and ishfāq is solicitude mixed with fear, because the one who feels it (mushfiq) loves the one he feels it for (mushfaq ʿalayhi) and fears what may befall him; when it is made transitive with min, the sense of fear in it is more evident, and when with ʿalā, the sense of solicitude is more evident." Al-Samīn said: "al-shafaq is of two kinds, the red shafaq and the white shafaq; al-shafaq and al-shafaqa are two nouns for ishfāq." Abū Ḥayyān said: "al-shafaq is the redness after the setting of the sun, when the time of the last night prayer comes; it was said that its root is from the fineness of a thing; one says shayʾ mushfiq, i.e. it does not hold together because of its fineness, and from it ashfaqa ʿalayhi, his heart softened; al-shafaqa is the noun from al-ishfāq, and so too al-shafaq. The poet said:
تهوى حياتي وأهوى موتها شفقا ... والموت أكرم نزال على الحرم
(She wishes my life and I wish her death out of solicitude; and death is the most generous guest to the women's quarters.)"
The wording of al-Qāmūs: "al-shafaq (vowelled) is the redness on the horizon from sunset to the last night prayer, or to near it, or to near the darkness"; and this is the sound view. From it is the poet's saying:
قم يا غلام أعنّي غير مرتبك ... على الزمان بكأس حشوها شفق
(Rise, boy, and help me, unflustered, against time with a cup whose filling is shafaq.)
(وَسَقَ): he gathered and joined. One says wasaqahu, so it was gathered (infasaqa) and became gathered (istawsaqa); its parallel in the occurrence of ifʿaʿala and istafʿala as reflexives is ittasaʿa and istawsaʿa. In al-Qāmūs: "wasaqahu yasiquhu (of the pattern ḍaraba): he gathered it and carried it; and from it ﴿وَاللَّيْلِ وَما وَسَقَ﴾."
(اتَّسَقَ): it gathered and became even on the night of the fourteenth. Al-Farrāʾ said: "it is its fullness and evenness on the nights of the full moon," and it is ifʿaʿala from al-wasq, which is joining and gathering, as above; and "so-and-so's affair is muttasiq," i.e. gathered upon what pleases.

* I'rab:
(فَلا أُقْسِمُ بِالشَّفَقِ وَاللَّيْلِ وَما وَسَقَ وَالْقَمَرِ إِذَا اتَّسَقَ لَتَرْكَبُنَّ طَبَقاً عَنْ طَبَقٍ): the fāʾ is the eloquent fāʾ (fāʾ faṣīḥa), because it stands in the apodosis of a preceding condition, i.e. "if you have known this," or "if you are certain of the return by resurrection, then I do not swear." The discussion of لا أُقْسِمُ has already preceded, so renew your acquaintance with it. بِالشَّفَقِ is attached to أُقْسِمُ; اللَّيْلِ is conjoined to الشَّفَقِ and the wāw is a conjunction; ما may be a relative noun, or an indefinite described noun, or a maṣdar particle. If it is relative or indefinite described, the returning pronoun of the ṣila or description is omitted, i.e. "wasaqahu," "gathered it." The meaning is the gathering of what had been dispersed by day of the kinds of creatures and species of beings, for each of them returns at night to its shelter. الْقَمَرِ is likewise conjoined; إذا is an adverbial void of the sense of condition, attached to the verb of oath, i.e. the time of its fullness and evenness; the lām is the response to the oath; لَتَرْكَبُنَّ is an imperfect verb in the nominative with the nūn dropped on account of the succession of similar letters, as it is one of the five verbs, and the omitted wāw, dropped through the meeting of two quiescents, is the agent, and the nūn is the heavy nūn of emphasis; طَبَقاً is a ḥāl or a direct object; and عَنْ طَبَقٍ, i.e. a community of people, is an adjective of طَبَقاً, i.e. a class passing beyond a class. On طَبَقاً being a direct object, there is an omitted muḍāf, i.e. "you will surely ride the ways, or the path, of class after class." Al-Zamakhsharī's wording: "If you say, what is the position of عَنْ طَبَقٍ? I say: accusative as an adjective of طَبَقاً, i.e. a class passing beyond a class, or a ḥāl from the pronoun in لَتَرْكَبُنَّ, i.e. you will ride a class, passing beyond a class (or 'passing' or 'passed') according to the reading." Al-Zamakhsharī also said: "It was read latarkabanna addressing the human being in ﴿يا أَيُّهَا الْإِنْسانُ﴾; latarkabunna with damma addressing the genus, because the address is to the genus; latarkabinna with kasra addressing the soul; and layarkabanna with yāʾ, 'the human being will surely ride.' Al-ṭabaq is what corresponds to another; one says 'this is not ṭabaq to that,' i.e. it does not correspond to it, and from it the cover is called al-ṭabaq, and iṭbāq al-tharā is what is layered of it; then the state corresponding to another was called ṭabaq, and from it the words of the Mighty and Majestic ﴿طَبَقاً عَنْ طَبَقٍ﴾, i.e. state after state, each corresponding to its sister in severity and terror. It may also be the plural of ṭabaqa, which is a rank, from their saying 'he is on ranks'; from it ṭabaq al-ẓahr for the vertebrae, the singular being ṭabaqa, in the sense 'you will ride states after states which are ranks of severity, some higher than others, namely death and what follows of the stations of the Resurrection and its terrors.'" I say: among the uses of al-ṭabaq in the sense of a community is the saying of al-ʿAbbās ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib about the Messenger of Allah ﷺ:
وأنت لما ولدت أشرقت الأر ... ض وضاءت بنورك الأفق
تنقل من صالب إلى رحم ... إذا مضى عالم بدا طبق
(When you were born the earth shone, and the horizon was lit by your light. You are moved from loin to womb; when one age passes, another community appears.)
(فَما لَهُمْ لا يُؤْمِنُونَ): the fāʾ is the eloquent fāʾ; ما is an interrogative noun, mubtadaʾ; لَهُمْ is the khabar; the clause لا يُؤْمِنُونَ is a ḥāl. (وَإِذا قُرِئَ عَلَيْهِمُ الْقُرْآنُ لا يَسْجُدُونَ): the clause is conjoined to the preceding circumstantial clause; إذا is a future adverbial containing the sense of a condition; the clause قُرِئَ is in the position of a genitive by the annexation of the adverbial to it; الْقُرْآنُ is the deputy agent; the clause لا يَسْجُدُونَ has no grammatical position because it is the apodosis of a non-jussive conditional. (بَلِ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا يُكَذِّبُونَ): بل is a particle of transitional rejection; الَّذِينَ is a mubtadaʾ; the clause كَفَرُوا has no position because it is the ṣila of الَّذِينَ; the clause يُكَذِّبُونَ is the khabar of الَّذِينَ. (وَاللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ بِما يُوعُونَ): the wāw is a conjunction; اللَّهُ is a mubtadaʾ and أَعْلَمُ its khabar; بِما is attached to أَعْلَمُ; the clause يُوعُونَ has no position because it is the ṣila of ما, i.e. what they hold in their hearts of denial. (فَبَشِّرْهُمْ بِعَذابٍ أَلِيمٍ): an imperative verb, a latent agent and a direct object; بِعَذابٍ is attached to بَشِّرْهُمْ and أَلِيمٍ is a naʿt. (إِلَّا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وَعَمِلُوا الصَّالِحاتِ لَهُمْ أَجْرٌ غَيْرُ مَمْنُونٍ): إلا is a particle of exception, and the exception is disconnected (munqaṭiʿ), meaning "but" (lākin); الَّذِينَ is a mubtadaʾ; the clause آمَنُوا is a ṣila; وَعَمِلُوا الصَّالِحاتِ is conjoined to the ṣila, within its scope; لَهُمْ is a fronted khabar and أَجْرٌ a deferred mubtadaʾ; غَيْرُ مَمْنُونٍ is a naʿt, i.e. not cut off nor diminished; and the nominal clause is the khabar of الَّذِينَ. It is also permissible for the exception to be connected (muttasil), in which case الَّذِينَ is the excepted.

* Rhetoric:
In «والليل وما وسق والقمر إذا اتسق» there is the art of iltizām, or luzūm mā lā yalzam (the obligation of what is not obligatory), which some call iʿnāt. It has been alluded to before: that the poet in his verse and the prose-writer in his prose binds himself to one letter or two or more before the rhyme letter, as far as he is able, on condition that there be no strain. We said that Abū al-ʿAlāʾ al-Maʿarrī has a dīwān in which he bound himself to what is not obligatory. As for the verse, the nūn is observed before the qāf.
